theory.intro: A scatter plot can be described using three separate features. Form asks whether the points loosely follow a straight line (a correlation) or a curve. Strength asks how closely the points cluster around a line of best fit. Direction asks whether the values move together or opposite each other as one variable increases.
facts: An association is any relationship between two numerical variables. A linear association — where the points loosely follow a straight line — is called a correlation.

Direction is positive when both variables increase together (an upward trend) and negative when one increases as the other decreases (a downward trend). Points scattered with no trend at all show zero correlation.
Strength describes how close the points sit to a line of best fit: strong (little scatter), moderate (some scatter), or weak (points widely spread from the line).

Form describes the overall shape of the pattern: linear (a straight-line pattern) or non-linear (a curved pattern). 'Correlation' specifically means a linear association — a clear curved pattern is a non-linear association, not a correlation.
steps: Look at the trend to decide the direction: positive, negative, or zero
Judge how closely the points sit to a line of best fit to decide the strength: strong, moderate or weak
Check whether the points follow a straight line or a curve to decide the form: linear or non-linear

mastery.question_text: Coach A's scatter plot of training hours against race time shows a strong negative correlation. Coach B's scatter plot of the same variables shows a weak negative correlation. Both coaches want to use a line of best fit to predict a runner's race time from their training hours. Whose predictions are likely to be more accurate, and why?
mastery.solution_text:
Coach A's data lies closer to the line of best fit, because the correlation is strong.
Coach B's data is more scattered away from the line, because the correlation is weak.
Coach A's predictions are likely to be more accurate, because points closer to the line mean less error between the actual and predicted race times.

The points don't form a straight line — they follow a curve that drops steeply and then levels off.
"Correlation" specifically describes a linear association, so a curved pattern should not be called a correlation.
A better description: a strong, negative, non-linear association.

Squad A's points sit very close to the line of best fit, showing a strong correlation.
Squad B's points are more spread out from the line, showing a moderate correlation.
Squad A's line of best fit would let you make more confident predictions, because there is less scatter away from the line.
